Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
There is something about me that made the event happen

vignette:
Ricardo, a 53-year-old tax consultant, had his life irrevocably altered several years ago during a protest. Caught in a volatile crowd and mistaken for someone else, he was severely beaten by officers, sustaining a broken arm and several fractured ribs. The brutal assault left him with chronic pain in his left side, and the vivid images of others around him suffering similar fates were seared into his memory. This single event shattered his once-firm belief in order and justice, replacing it with a pervasive sense of dread.

In the immediate aftermath, Ricardo found himself wrestling with a landscape of internal and external reminders. A dull, persistent ache in his left side, a somatic pain that never truly vanished, became a potent trigger, instantly transporting him back to the moment of impact and the feeling of helplessness. He also became acutely sensitive to any visible injuries or wounds on others; a client's bandaged hand or a character's bruise on a TV show would trigger a wave of nausea and a tightening in his chest. Perhaps most distressing were the victim memories that would flood his mind whenever he encountered news of police brutality or a memorial, bringing back not just his own terror but the haunted faces of those who suffered alongside him.

These recurring triggers began to profoundly reshape Ricardo's perception of himself and his place in the world. When he encountered a visible injury or felt that familiar ache in his side, he would often find himself spiraling into the conviction that there was something intrinsically faulty about him, a fundamental weakness or defect that had made the event happen, or at least made him uniquely susceptible to it. He started to feel profoundly isolated and set apart from others, believing that no one could truly understand the horror he had endured or the constant internal battle he faced. This growing sense of alienation, coupled with the persistent reminders of his trauma, led him to question if his life was even worth living anymore, feeling trapped in a world that no longer felt safe or meaningful.

This deep-seated belief that his life might not be worth living, and the internal conviction that he was intrinsically faulty, fueled a pervasive sense of vulnerability. Ricardo became convinced that he was constantly in danger, an easy target in an unpredictable world. As a result, his threat monitoring escalated dramatically. He began to avoid going to unfamiliar places, explaining to himself that he simply couldn't assess the danger effectively in new environments, and it was better to stick to the known, however small his world became. Before he could feel comfortable anywhere, even in a familiar client's office, he would always identify potential escape routes, mentally mapping exits and choke points in an unconscious but relentless ritual.

His constant vigilance, the relentless checking behind him in the street, and his heightened awareness of his surroundings paradoxically made him even more sensitive to potential triggers. His internal alarm system, always on high alert for danger, would immediately seize upon any minor visual cue-a slightly limping pedestrian, a fleeting grimace on someone's face that might suggest a visible injury-and interpret it as a direct threat or a potent reminder of the violence he experienced. The physical pain in his side, often dull, would sharpen under this intense scrutiny, becoming a more intrusive and immediate reminder of the trauma.

Over time, this relentless threat monitoring and the associated avoidance behaviors began to reinforce his negative appraisals. The very act of always identifying escape routes and needing to check behind him made him feel more and more isolated. He found himself unable to relax in social settings, constantly scanning the room, which further cemented his belief that he was fundamentally different from others, unable to experience normal life. This growing isolation and the feeling of being perpetually on guard deepened his conviction that his life was not worth living, as it was now defined by fear and vigilance rather than connection and purpose. His work as a tax consultant, which once involved meeting a diverse range of clients, became increasingly challenging. He found himself declining new clients whose offices were in unfamiliar parts of the city, preferring to work remotely or only with established clients in his known circuit, which began to impact his professional growth and income.

Ricardo recently realized the extent to which his life had shrunk. His divorce, finalized two years prior, left him living alone, and his social circle had withered as he pushed away friends who suggested outings to new restaurants or unfamiliar parks. He now finds himself spending most evenings alone, questioning the value of his existence. It was this profound sense of emptiness, coupled with a growing fear that he would never feel safe again, that finally compelled him to seek help, hoping to reclaim a life that felt meaningful beyond the constant shadow of danger and his own perceived brokenness.
